During the Q3 2025 call, with revenue already running 23 percent below the prior-year quarter, the acknowledgement was equally direct: "The demand upturn has not yet materialized in Q3/2025." He accompanied that admission with a structural claim: "medium- and long-term growth drivers, e.g. with the introduction of new 800V architectures for AI data centers using both SiC and GaN, remain intact." Whether the cycle has turned by the frozen snapshot date of May 2026 is addressed in the financials chapter; the point here is that Grawert operates with a publicly stated conviction about the end-market trajectory that he has not walked back through the downcycle.

## The Supervisory Board: Industry Credentials Rebuilt Around Semiconductors

Germany's two-tier governance model places the Aufsichtsrat — Supervisory Board — in a constitutionally distinct oversight role from the operating Vorstand. AIXTRON's six-member Supervisory Board, as constituted by the 2025 annual general meeting, has been substantially refreshed since the post-LED-cycle restructuring years.

The most consequential recent change was the election of Alexander Everke as chairman following Kim Schindelhauer's resignation at the 2025 AGM. Everke, who served as CEO of ams-OSRAM AG from 2016 until handing over to Aldo Kamper in early 2023, had grown that company from approximately €500m in annual revenue to roughly €5bn, principally through the acquisition of OSRAM and a strategic pivot toward optical sensing and automotive photonics. His sector biography — Siemens, Infineon, NXP, ams-OSRAM — maps almost directly onto AIXTRON's customer base and growth markets. He chairs both the Nomination and Capital Market committees. [Semiconductor Today, February 2025](https://www.semiconductor-today.com/news_items/2025/feb/aixtron-270225.shtml)

Deputy chairman Frits van Hout, on the board since 2019, brings a complementary perspective: a career that included executive roles at ASML, the Dutch lithography incumbent whose capital-equipment business model and customer-concentration dynamics are structurally familiar to AIXTRON's situation, albeit at a different scale. Van Hout chairs the Remuneration Committee.

The remaining four members span audit, technology operations, and capital-markets expertise. Ingo Bank — CFO of City Football Group and formerly CFO of ams-OSRAM, OSRAM Licht, and Philips — joined in 2025 alongside Everke, deepening the semiconductor-adjacent financial oversight on the board. Dr. Stefan Traeger, ~~chairman of JENOPTIK AG's Vorstand since May 2022~~ ==who became JENOPTIK AG's Chairman of the Executive Board / President & CEO on May 1, 2017, and whose departure from JENOPTIK's Executive Board effective February 15, 2026 had been announced before the snapshot date==, brought optical and photonics industrial perspective. Karen Florschütz, executive vice president at Airbus Defence and Space with prior Siemens operations background, has served since 2024. Prof. Dr. Anna Weber of Heilbronn University chairs the Audit Committee and also sits on the Supervisory Board of Wacker Chemie AG, a Munich-listed specialty-chemicals producer with meaningful semiconductor materials exposure.

| Member | Role | Board since | Background anchor |
|---|---|---|---|
| Alexander Everke | Chairman | 2025 | CEO ams-OSRAM, Infineon, NXP |
| Frits van Hout | Deputy Chairman | 2019 | ASML executive, Oxford MA |
| Ingo Bank | Member | 2025 | CFO ams-OSRAM / OSRAM / Philips |
| Karen Florschütz | Member | 2024 | EVP Airbus Defence and Space; Siemens |
| Dr. Stefan Traeger | Member | 2022 | ~~Chairman, JENOPTIK AG Vorstand~~ ==Former Chairman of the Executive Board / President & CEO, JENOPTIK AG== |
| Prof. Dr. Anna Weber | Member (Audit chair) | 2019 | Heilbronn University; Wacker Chemie |

The concentration of ams-OSRAM alumni — Everke and Bank both served there, as CFO and CEO respectively — at the top of the Supervisory Board in 2025 was the most visible signal of where the board believed AIXTRON's strategic reference points lay: not in legacy LED equipment or generic industrial capital equipment, but in the compound-semiconductor photonics and power-electronics complex that connects MOCVD deposition to AI infrastructure, automotive electrification, and optical datacom. Whether that strategic alignment translates into order-book execution over the remainder of the decade is the question Grawert and Danninger are contracted to answer.

chapters.title: Power, photonics, and display device-maker customers plus the Herzogenrath manufacturing footprint
chapters.body:
The device makers who defined the compound-semiconductor frontier sorted, through the period 2020–2025, into three broadly distinct buying clusters around AIXTRON's MOCVD platforms: GaN power electronics foundries and integrated device manufacturers building capacity for the energy transition; SiC power device makers entering a competitive epi-tool landscape; and the photonics supply chain serving datacom, automotive LiDAR, and 3D sensing. A fourth cluster — micro-LED display — held out the largest potential ticket size but, at the frozen snapshot date, the least confirmed order flow.

## GaN Power Electronics: The Core Customer Bloc

The anchoring customers for AIXTRON's G5+ and G10-GaN platforms spanned both European integrated device manufacturers and a fast-expanding Chinese foundry ecosystem. Infineon Technologies, headquartered in Munich and among the world's largest power-semiconductor companies, built out GaN-on-Si capacity for its CoolGaN product family — an effort serving automotive traction inverters, data-centre power supplies, and industrial motor drives. STMicroelectronics, the Franco-Italian IDM, similarly expanded GaN epitaxy capacity as it pursued market position in 600V and 650V GaN device families. Both companies are established AIXTRON accounts whose capital programmes tracked the broader automotive-electrification and data-centre-power cycles.

Further up the risk curve, fabless and fab-lite GaN specialists — Navitas Semiconductor, EPC (Efficient Power Conversion), Power Integrations — represent a class of customer whose own growth depends on contracted wafer supply from GaN foundries that themselves run AIXTRON tools. GaN Systems, the Ottawa-based pure-play GaN power designer, was acquired by Infineon in 2023, consolidating engineering talent and capital-expenditure decision-making into a larger pool that remained aligned with the AIXTRON platform.

The most consequential new GaN customer geography, however, was China. Innoscience, a Zhuhai-based GaN-on-Si foundry backed by significant state-adjacent capital, emerged through 2022–2024 as one of the most aggressive capacity builders in the global GaN foundry landscape. The company's buildout of 8-inch GaN-on-Si capacity explicitly targeted consumer fast-charging, photovoltaic inverters, and data-centre power conversion — a ramp that translated into meaningful AIXTRON equipment orders. China's broader policy emphasis on domestic semiconductor self-sufficiency gave a structural tailwind to this activity that showed little sign of abating through the frozen snapshot window, even as export-control scrutiny across the wider semiconductor supply chain intensified.

AIXTRON's annual report and investor communications confirmed that power electronics — principally GaN — had become the single largest revenue contributor in the equipment mix by the mid-2020s, having displaced LED MOCVD tools as the dominant product line during the prior cycle.

## SiC Power Epitaxy: Entering a Contested Landscape

The G10-SiC platform, commercialised through 2023–2024, brought AIXTRON into direct competition with established SiC epi-tool suppliers including Veeco Instruments, as well as with purpose-built SiC specialists that had historically dominated silicon-carbide homoepitaxial growth. The SiC power device market itself ~~was expanding rapidly~~ ==had expanded rapidly before overcapacity made 2026 demand weak==, driven by EV traction inverter adoption — Tesla, BYD, and the European automotive OEM supply chains had collectively pulled forward enormous SiC demand — and Wolfspeed, the Cree spin-off, stood as the most prominent customer archetype: a vertically integrated SiC device maker racing to bring its Siler City, North Carolina mega-fab into full production.

STMicroelectronics appeared on both sides of the relevant customer map — it is among the world's largest SiC device makers and had disclosed capital-expenditure commitments running into the billions of dollars for SiC wafer and epi capacity expansion through 2027–2028. Whether AIXTRON's G10-SiC platform captured meaningful share of that spend was, at the snapshot date, only partly disclosed; the company acknowledged customer qualification processes and initial shipments but had not publicly named specific SiC accounts with the granularity it applied to its GaN customer relationships.

## Photonics: Datacom Lasers, VCSELs, and the Apple Tier-1 Supply Chain

AIXTRON's GaAs and InP MOCVD platforms — the older, more mature portion of the business — continued to serve the photonics supply chain with equipment for laser diodes, VCSELs, and high-electron-mobility transistor structures. Coherent Corp (formed by the 2022 combination of II-VI Incorporated and the legacy Coherent), Lumentum Holdings, Sumitomo Electric Industries, and Mitsubishi Electric represented the principal tier-1 device makers in this segment.

The VCSEL sub-segment commanded sustained attention because of its centrality to 3D sensing — specifically in the structured-light and time-of-flight proximity systems deployed in premium smartphones. Apple's Face ID module, which draws VCSELs sourced through tier-1 suppliers including Lumentum and II-VI/Coherent, became an indirect demand signal for AIXTRON tools, since those suppliers' capacity expansions required MOCVD epi platforms. Apple does not appear on any AIXTRON customer list directly; the relationship is architecturally buried two or three supply-chain tiers deep, visible in aggregate capital-expenditure flows rather than named accounts.

Automotive LiDAR added a second photonics growth vector. The expansion of production-intent LiDAR systems across the automotive OEM supply chain — through suppliers including Luminar, Innoviz, and Valeo — drove demand for pulsed-laser-diode and VCSEL capacity that fed back to the same tier-1 photonics device makers running AIXTRON tools.

## Micro-LED Display: The Thesis That Stalled

No segment of AIXTRON's prospective customer base generated more investor discussion between 2021 and 2024 — and delivered less confirmed production-scale revenue — than micro-LED display. The thesis centred on display panel makers, principally Korean (Samsung Display, LG Display) and Taiwanese (AUO, PlayNitride), needing high-throughput GaN MOCVD capacity to produce micro-LED epitaxial wafers for next-generation emissive displays. Apple's reported development of a micro-LED Apple Watch Ultra module was the most-cited demand anchor; its reported cancellation or indefinite delay in early 2024 materially reset the investment community's timeline expectations for the segment.

AIXTRON management was measured in characterising micro-LED order timing throughout this period, noting that customer development activity continued — research tools and pilot-line equipment were in the field — but that mass-production capacity orders had not materialised at the volumes originally anticipated. The gap between pilot-line hardware and the production-scale order book defined the segment's posture at the snapshot date: present in R&D budgets, absent from volume revenues.

## Geographic Mix and Export-Control Exposure

AIXTRON's revenue has historically carried a pronounced Asian weighting, with China, Taiwan, South Korea, and Japan collectively accounting for the majority of equipment deliveries in most fiscal years. China alone, at peak LED MOCVD cycle volumes in the 2010s, exceeded half of group revenue in certain periods. Through the GaN power cycle of 2022–2024, China remained the single largest country revenue contributor — driven by Innoscience and the broader domestic GaN foundry buildout — though the proportional share moderated as European and North American GaN capacity orders grew.

| Region | Principal customer types | Demand driver |
|--------|--------------------------|---------------|
| China | GaN foundries (Innoscience et al.) | Domestic semi policy, consumer/solar power |
| Taiwan | Display, photonics | Micro-LED pilots, VCSEL |
| South Korea | Display OEMs | Micro-LED R&D |
| Japan | Photonics (Sumitomo, Mitsubishi) | Datacom, automotive LiDAR |
| North America | Wolfspeed (SiC), Navitas, EPC | EV, data centre |
| Europe | Infineon, STMicro | Automotive, industrial |

This China exposure drew sustained attention from AIXTRON's investor base and from German and European regulators. MOCVD equipment did not fall, through the snapshot date, within the most tightly controlled categories of the U.S. Commerce Department's Export Administration Regulations as applied to advanced logic and memory fabs. But compound-semiconductor epi tools occupy a grey zone in dual-use export control frameworks. AIXTRON applied for and received export licences on a transaction-by-transaction basis for sensitive end-users, disclosing compliance costs without quantifying lost-order exposure from licence denials. The October 2023 and subsequent expansions of U.S. advanced-chip export controls created a durable overhang: AIXTRON's GaN and SiC tools served power and photonics applications that remained outside the most stringent controls as of the snapshot date, but the regulatory trajectory pointed toward progressive tightening. Any future extension of compound-semiconductor controls into the GaN power device supply chain would directly affect Innoscience and comparable Chinese foundry customers.

## The Herzogenrath Footprint

AIXTRON's manufacturing and engineering operations are concentrated in Herzogenrath, a small city on Germany's western border with the Netherlands, adjacent to Aachen and within the ~~RWTH Aachen technology corridor from which the company was spun out in 1983~~ ==Aachen technology corridor where the company was founded in 1983 by employees of RWTH Aachen's Institute for Semiconductor Technology==. The Herzogenrath site hosts the core competencies: reactor engineering and design, software and process-control development, and the final assembly and functional test of MOCVD systems before customer delivery.

The capital-light character of that model — design-and-assemble rather than vertically integrated fabrication — means that critical system components are sourced from a global tier-one supplier base. Quartz and ceramic reactor components, gas delivery systems, vacuum hardware, and precision mechanical assemblies are procured from specialist suppliers across Germany, the wider EU, and, in selected categories, Asia. AIXTRON does not operate a high-volume manufacturing floor in the conventional sense; each MOCVD tool is a capital-intensive, precision-engineered system assembled to customer specification and fully characterised before shipment.

The company expanded its Herzogenrath footprint in response to the order-intake surge accompanying the GaN power ramp of 2022–2024, adding cleanroom test and assembly capacity to compress the interval from order to delivery. A smaller R&D and engineering facility in ~~Abingdon, Oxfordshire — a legacy of earlier UK acquisitions~~ ==Swavesey, Cambridge — rooted in the 1999 acquisition of Thomas Swan Scientific Equipment== — supplemented the German base on platform-level reactor innovation. Headcount in engineering, manufacturing, and service at the German site remained the structural cost core; the company's relatively high gross margins, characteristic of capital-equipment businesses with significant aftermarket service and spares revenue, reflected the design-intensive rather than fabrication-intensive character of the Herzogenrath operation.

chapters.title: Where AIXTRON sits against Veeco plus the broader MOCVD and compound-semi equipment set
chapters.body:
## The Duopoly That Survived the LED Bust

The global market for compound-semiconductor deposition equipment resolved, through the LED super-cycle and its brutal aftermath, into an effective duopoly. At its peak, AIXTRON and Veeco Instruments together commanded roughly 80–90 percent of the world's MOCVD tool revenue. The Chinese LED boom that swelled both companies to record backlogs in 2011 also planted the seeds of competitive disruption that followed. A decade later, with AIXTRON refocused on power electronics and photonics and Veeco similarly repositioned, the rivalry persisted on new terrain—GaN power epitaxy, SiC epitaxy, and advanced photonics—while a cohort of Chinese state-backed equipment makers absorbed the commodity LED segment the incumbents had vacated.

## The Veeco Rivalry: From LED Wars to Power Electronics

Veeco Instruments (NASDAQ: VECO), headquartered in Plainview, New York, is AIXTRON's most direct and most consequential competitor. The two firms traded market-share wins and losses in MOCVD from at least the mid-2000s, and any assessment of AIXTRON's competitive position begins and ends there.

During the 2009–2012 LED equipment boom—when mainland Chinese LED chipmakers were racing to bring down the cost of solid-state lighting on state subsidy—both companies saw order intake surge to levels neither had experienced before. AIXTRON's revenues ~~peaked above €700m~~ ==reached €783.8m in FY2010 before falling to €611.0m in FY2011==; Veeco crossed $500m in revenue in 2011. The busts were correspondingly severe. By 2014–2015 both were reporting revenues a fraction of the earlier peak as Chinese LED manufacturers sat on overcapacity and halted capex.

The strategic responses then diverged. Veeco moved into adjacent markets through M&A: its $769m acquisition of Ultratech in 2017 added laser annealing and advanced-packaging capabilities, diversifying away from pure MOCVD dependency. AIXTRON remained more narrowly focused on MOCVD and related chemical vapour deposition equipment—a focus the post-2020 compound-semiconductor transition would ultimately vindicate.

By 2023, AIXTRON reported revenues of ~~approximately €629m~~ ==€629.9m==, with order intake still reflecting strong GaN power demand across automotive and data-centre customers. Veeco's consolidated revenues for the same period came in near $600m, though a significant portion now derived from Ion Beam technology and semiconductor processing equipment unrelated to MOCVD. On a like-for-like MOCVD basis, the two companies remained close in scale.

## Platform Comparison: G10-GaN versus Propel

The sharpest competitive battleground through 2023–2025 was GaN-on-Si epitaxy for power-electronics applications—the transistors and diodes going into data-centre power supplies, electric-vehicle chargers, and consumer adapters. AIXTRON's answer was the G10-GaN, a large-footprint planetary reactor offering high throughput for 150mm and 200mm GaN-on-Si wafers. Veeco's competitive tool was the Propel platform, a cluster architecture designed to deliver tight uniformity at volume.

The architectural difference was not cosmetic. AIXTRON's planetary-reactor heritage, inherited from the LED era, spread multiple wafers across a rotating susceptor, prioritising throughput in a production context. Veeco's Propel adopted a different geometry that its engineers argued delivered superior within-wafer uniformity—a claim resonating with customers targeting tight threshold-voltage distributions in power devices. The practical result was segmented adoption: AIXTRON tended to win at higher-volume commodity power customers, particularly across East Asia; Veeco had success with customers demanding the tightest specifications for automotive and data-centre power.

| Feature | AIXTRON G10-GaN | Veeco Propel GaN |
|---|---|---|
| Reactor architecture | Multi-wafer planetary (batch) | Cluster, single-run geometry |
| Target wafer sizes | 150 mm / 200 mm GaN-on-Si | 150 mm / 200 mm GaN-on-Si |
| Throughput profile | High batch throughput | Flexibility and uniformity emphasis |
| Geographic strength | Asia-Pacific, European Tier 1s | North America, diversified |
| SiC epi sibling | G10-SiC | Lumina SiC |

For SiC epitaxy—a newer battleground as the power-device industry expanded SiC adoption for EV inverters—the rivalry replicated itself at the platform level. AIXTRON's G10-SiC entered commercial qualification in the 2023–2025 period against Veeco's Lumina SiC platform and the established presence of LPE (Laboratorio di Progettazione Elettronico), the Milan-based specialist that had supplied SiC epi reactors to Wolfspeed and STMicroelectronics before AIXTRON entered the market. Applied Materials also held presence in SiC epitaxy CVD equipment, bringing a balance-sheet scale and customer-integration reach that neither AIXTRON nor Veeco could easily match. AIXTRON's G10-SiC entry was credible but late into a segment where LPE and Applied Materials already held qualification reference sites.

## Chinese MOCVD: A Contained but Funded Threat

The most visible competitive shift of the post-LED decade was the rise of Chinese domestic MOCVD equipment makers. Advanced Micro-Fabrication Equipment China (AMEC, 中微公司), listed on Shanghai's STAR Market, became China's flagship plasma-etch equipment supplier—but its MOCVD capabilities remained a secondary business line through 2025, more relevant for LED-era applications than for the high-specification compound-semiconductor work where AIXTRON competes. NAURA Technology Group (北方华创), a broader semiconductor equipment conglomerate, similarly maintained MOCVD tools in its portfolio alongside etch, furnace, and PVD equipment, but its MOCVD franchise did not penetrate the advanced power and photonics segments in a meaningful way before the frozen snapshot date.

What Chinese equipment makers did accomplish was the wholesale displacement of AIXTRON and Veeco from the commodity LED MOCVD market inside China. By the early 2020s, leading domestic LED producers—Sanan Optoelectronics, Huacan, and others—were procuring Chinese tools at lower price points for marginal capacity additions. AIXTRON effectively conceded that segment and did not contest it at low margin.

The more consequential question, unresolved as of May 2026, was whether AMEC, NAURA, or newer entrants could qualify for GaN power or SiC epi applications at the specification levels demanded by automotive Tier 1 suppliers. The answer, so far, was no—but the trajectory warranted monitoring. Chinese government industrial policy made compound-semiconductor self-sufficiency an explicit objective. The capability gap was real; so was the capital flowing toward closing it.

## Photonics: Niche Depth as a Defensive Moat

In photonics-grade MOCVD—InP-based laser diodes for datacom transceivers, GaAs VCSELs for 3D sensing, and tools for photonic integrated circuits—AIXTRON occupied territory where the competitive set narrowed considerably. Veeco retained a presence in photonics MOCVD, but the research and low-volume tiers were served by smaller specialists: Agnitron Technology in the United States ~~and Thomas Swan in Cambridge—both research-tool vendors lacking the production scale to threaten~~ ==and other niche suppliers lacking the production scale to threaten== AIXTRON's volume relationships with II-VI/Coherent, Lumentum, Sumitomo Electric, and Mitsubishi Electric. ==AIXTRON's Cambridge presence was its own AIXTRON Ltd operation, rooted in the 1999 Thomas Swan Scientific Equipment acquisition.==

The photonics segment mattered strategically because it provided revenue diversity that partially cushioned the cyclicality of the power-electronics capex cycle. Datacom laser orders—driven by hyperscaler data-centre build-out and AI-related optical-interconnect demand—sustained photonics MOCVD bookings through periods when power-device capex softened. Grawert signalled in commentary around the 2024 results period that photonics remained a structurally resilient portion of the order pipeline even as micro-LED uncertainty weighed on headline intake.

## Strategic Position: Structural Advantages and Exposed Flanks

AIXTRON's competitive position as of the frozen date rested on several structural advantages unlikely to erode quickly. European regulatory and customer relationships in automotive-grade qualification cycles—Infineon, STMicroelectronics, Bosch—favoured suppliers with established process history and local engineering support. AIXTRON's Herzogenrath base and German engineering culture aligned with Tier 1 automotive supply-chain norms in ways that a US or Chinese competitor found difficult to replicate through price alone. The G10 platform architecture, refined across multiple compound-semiconductor applications from GaN-on-Si to SiC to photonics, gave AIXTRON process-engineering depth that Chinese challengers had not yet replicated for power-grade applications. And the installed base of tools already operating at customer fabs—generating spares, process licenses, and upgrade revenue—provided a financial floor that new entrants could not access quickly.

The vulnerabilities were equally legible. The micro-LED display thesis, which had powered a meaningful portion of AIXTRON's 2021–2022 order surge, deflated sharply after reports of the Apple Watch micro-LED programme cancellation or delay surfaced in early 2024. That single application had represented a potential step-change in the MOCVD addressable market; its deferral removed an order catalyst that had been partially priced into expectations across the install base. The GaN power inventory digestion cycle of 2024 compounded the order-intake pressure, leaving AIXTRON navigating a simultaneous pause in two of its highest-growth vectors.

Chinese equipment makers' funded ambition to close the specification gap in power MOCVD remained a long-duration risk, even if it was not yet a near-term revenue threat. And Veeco—a well-capitalised competitor with its own platform evolution roadmap and a broader revenue base to sustain R&D through downturns—retained the capacity to win at premium specification nodes if its Propel architecture continued to demonstrate uniformity advantages at 200mm.

The duopoly that emerged from the LED era survived into the power-electronics transition. But it operated on more contested, application-specific terrain than the uniform LED-chipmaker capex cycle had once provided—and AIXTRON's ability to hold its position in each sub-segment rested on engineering reputation that required constant replenishment.

chapters.title: Timeline from 1983 founding through GaN power inflection and micro-LED reset
chapters.body:
## From the Aachen Laboratory to the GaN Inflection

AIXTRON was incorporated in 1983 as ~~a commercial spin-off from RWTH Aachen University and the Max Planck Institute~~ ==a company founded by employees of the Institute for Semiconductor Technology at RWTH Aachen==, translating academic research into metal-organic chemical vapor deposition reactors for the compound-semiconductor industry. The company planted itself in Herzogenrath, a small city in North Rhine-Westphalia that sits literally on the Belgian border, and never relocated. For its first two decades it occupied a narrow specialist position, supplying MOCVD equipment to makers of gallium arsenide and indium phosphide devices — the optoelectronic substrate for telecommunications lasers, early mobile handset chips, and satellite amplifiers. Revenue was modest, cyclical, and dependent on the capital expenditure rhythms of a handful of tier-one device fabs in Japan, Europe, and the United States.

The company listed on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange in ~~1998~~ ==1997==, joining what would eventually become the ~~SDAX index and the TecDAX constellation~~ ==MDAX index and the TecDAX constellation== of German technology names. The listing gave AIXTRON access to growth capital at a moment when compound-semiconductor demand, particularly for GaAs power amplifiers in handsets, was just beginning to scale. But the defining commercial event of the company's first thirty years was not in power electronics — it was in lighting.

## The LED Cycle: Boom, Bust, and Strategic Reset

Between roughly 2008 and 2012, AIXTRON experienced its most explosive growth phase to that point, as LED lighting emerged as a mass-market replacement for incandescent and fluorescent bulbs. Blue-LED epitaxy required MOCVD reactors — the same core tool AIXTRON had supplied for decades — and the global rush to build LED production capacity created a multi-year equipment supercycle. Revenue rose sharply through 2010 and 2011, ~~reaching a peak that at the time represented a step-change from the company's historical trading range~~ ==with FY2010 revenue reaching €783.8 million before FY2011 revenue declined to €611.0 million==. Orders poured in from Taiwanese, Chinese, Korean, and European device makers, all racing to secure epitaxy capacity ahead of anticipated LED luminaire demand.

The correction was severe. From 2012, Chinese government subsidies underwrote a wave of domestic LED reactor procurement — much of it from local tool suppliers — while global LED chip supply quickly outpaced demand. Utilisation rates at customer fabs collapsed, and new MOCVD tool orders dried up across the industry. AIXTRON's revenue contracted substantially through 2013 and 2014, and the company entered a multi-year restructuring that forced a frank reassessment of its end-market exposure. The LED MOCVD chapter, while financially eventful, demonstrated a structural vulnerability: commodity end-markets and subsidy-distorted competition could erase years of growth within a single capital cycle.

## The 2016 Interruption: Chinese Bid and the Forced Pivot

Before the post-LED strategic repositioning could fully materialise, AIXTRON faced the most unusual episode in its history. In 2016, a consortium backed by Chinese state-linked capital — operating through FuJian Grand Chip Investment Fund GmbH — made a takeover bid for the company. The German government initially issued clearance under foreign-investment review, ~~but the transaction was subsequently blocked by the United States on national security grounds: President Obama invoked presidential authority under CFIUS review in December 2016, citing AIXTRON's work on compound-semiconductor technology with dual-use defence applications~~ ==then withdrew and reopened that clearance; the offer lapsed after the U.S. national-security review led President Obama to issue a December 2016 presidential order preventing the transaction condition from being met==. The episode was a landmark in the tightening of Western scrutiny over Chinese acquisition of semiconductor equipment firms, and it reverberated across the European industrial policy debate for years. For AIXTRON internally, the outcome — independence maintained, strategic trajectory unchanged — reinforced the imperative to diversify away from commoditised LED MOCVD and toward higher-value, defence-adjacent compound-semiconductor applications.

## The Grawert Era: Restructuring the Product Portfolio

Felix Grawert, who had arrived ~~from McKinsey in 2017 and joined the Executive Board as co-CEO alongside Bernd Schulte in 2018~~ ==from Infineon Technologies in 2017, joined the Executive Board in August 2017, and has been Chairman of the Executive Board, CEO & President since March 2021==, presided over the product portfolio's most consequential reshaping. The company identified three growth vectors that could sustain a durable capital-equipment franchise beyond the LED cycle: gallium nitride power electronics, silicon carbide power device epitaxy, and photonics tools for datacom laser diodes and VCSELs.

The G5 and G10 reactor platforms became the commercial articulation of that strategy. The G5 — a mid-throughput, flexible-wafer-configuration tool — addressed existing GaN-on-silicon and GaN-on-SiC epiwafer production for power device customers. The G10, a larger and higher-throughput platform, targeted the scale requirements of automotive-grade power conversion and data centre power delivery as those markets began to qualify GaN solutions. Both platforms were designed to serve a customer base that bore no structural resemblance to the LED fabs of the boom years: Infineon, STMicroelectronics, Navitas Semiconductor, Power Integrations, and China-based GaN specialists such as Innoscience. By 2023 the G10-GaN shipment ramp had become the principal revenue driver, coinciding with the first wave of meaningful automotive 800-volt architecture adoption and the rapid proliferation of GaN-based chargers in the consumer electronics market.

~~At the end of 2023, Bernd Schulte retired from the Executive Board after a tenure spanning multiple decades, leaving Grawert as sole CEO with CFO Christian Danninger as his principal board colleague. The transition was orderly, reflecting a succession that had been managed across the preceding five years of co-leadership.~~ ==Bernd Schulte's Executive Board tenure ended in March/April 2021, leaving Grawert as Chairman of the Executive Board, CEO & President with CFO Christian Danninger as his principal board colleague. The transition was orderly, reflecting a succession managed through the prior board reshaping.== AIXTRON reported fiscal 2024 revenues in excess of €600 million, a level that would have been unimaginable in the post-LED trough years.

## The SiC Entry and the Micro-LED Reset

The G10-SiC platform, commercialised through 2023 and 2024, positioned AIXTRON in the silicon carbide power epitaxy segment as a challenger to existing SiC epi equipment suppliers and vertically integrated incumbents. SiC-based power devices — dominant in electric vehicle inverters — require high-quality epitaxial layers whose uniformity and defect density directly determine device yield and reliability. AIXTRON entered a competitive landscape where it was not the established incumbent, but the G10-SiC represented a credible effort to apply the company's MOCVD process expertise to a market undergoing its own multi-year capital cycle.

Simultaneously, the micro-LED display thesis — once projected as a potentially transformational new end-market for MOCVD epitaxy — suffered a significant setback. Reports in early 2024 indicated that Apple's much-anticipated micro-LED programme for the Apple Watch had been cancelled or materially delayed, removing what had been a visible near-term demand catalyst for display-grade micro-LED epitaxy equipment. Through 2024 and into 2025, capacity orders for micro-LED display tools remained muted. The thesis was not abandoned — the physics of micro-LED efficiency and the long-term trajectory toward micro-LED automotive displays and eventually consumer panels remained technically credible — but the timeline receded materially.

## Forward Catalysts Through the 2026 Horizon

The compound-semiconductor capital cycle that frames AIXTRON's forward earnings trajectory rests on several concurrent adoption curves. ~~GaN power electronics continued to penetrate automotive onboard chargers, data centre switched-mode power supplies, and industrial motor drives through 2025, with the pace of qualification wins at tier-one automotive OEM suppliers and hyperscaler power infrastructure providers setting the near-term order cadence for G10-GaN reactors. SiC epitaxy demand remained structurally tied to electric vehicle production volumes and the speed at which incumbent SiC device makers expanded wafer capacity, a trajectory subject to inventory correction dynamics that surfaced across the power semiconductor supply chain in 2024. Photonics represented the third demand vector: laser diode and VCSEL tool demand from datacom transceiver manufacturers — themselves supplying the AI infrastructure buildout that defined data centre capital expenditure through 2025 — provided a near-term counterweight to the micro-LED softness.~~ ==As of the April 2026 update, optoelectronics was the main demand driver, supported by laser diode and VCSEL tool demand from datacom transceiver manufacturers supplying the AI infrastructure buildout that defined data centre capital expenditure through 2025. GaN power electronics remained stable to moderately improving across automotive onboard chargers, data centre switched-mode power supplies, and industrial motor drives, with the pace of qualification wins at tier-one automotive OEM suppliers and hyperscaler power infrastructure providers setting the order cadence for G10-GaN reactors. SiC epitaxy demand remained structurally tied to electric vehicle production volumes, but the near-term order environment was weak as overcapacity and inventory correction dynamics worked through the power semiconductor supply chain.== Micro-LED display remained the long-duration option: a genuinely large total addressable market if the display-grade yield and cost curve could be solved, with the timeline no longer anchored to a single consumer product launch.

chapters.title: MOCVD reactor IP, compound-semi process technology, R&D framework
chapters.body:
## Planetary Reactors and the Aachen Inheritance

AIXTRON's intellectual identity was forged at the intersection of ~~two German scientific institutions~~ ==RWTH Aachen's semiconductor-technology research ecosystem==. When the company ~~spun out of RWTH Aachen University and the Max Planck Institute~~ ==was founded in 1983 by employees of the Institute for Semiconductor Technology at RWTH Aachen==, its founders carried with them a specific conviction: that the deposition of compound-semiconductor thin films required not merely better chemistry but fundamentally better reactor geometry. That conviction shaped every tool generation that followed.

The core of AIXTRON's IP estate is the **Planetary Reactor** concept — a design in which individual wafer carriers, called satellites, rotate on their own axes while simultaneously orbiting a central axis on a large rotating susceptor. The compound motion is not decorative engineering; it is the mechanism that exposes each wafer to the same time-averaged gas composition and thermal environment. In metal-organic chemical vapor deposition, where epitaxial layer thicknesses are measured in nanometres and dopant concentrations must be controlled to parts per billion, uniformity is not a specification category but a yield-determining variable. AIXTRON's patent filings, accumulated across four decades, reflect an obsessive refinement of this central geometry — satellite design, gas-foil rotation (which allows wafers to float on a thin cushion of process gas, reducing particle generation), susceptor materials, and the thermal boundary conditions that govern growth kinetics.

Alongside the Planetary Reactor family, AIXTRON developed the **Close Coupled Showerhead (CCS)** architecture, used in its AIX 2600 G5 platform and adapted for ~~several optoelectronic applications~~ ==specific legacy and separately configured applications==. In the CCS design, the gas distribution plate sits in close proximity to the wafer surface, minimising the mixing length and enabling sharper compositional transitions between epitaxial layers — critical for heterojunction structures in laser diodes, VCSELs, and high-electron-mobility transistors. The two architectures — planetary susceptor and close-coupled showerhead — constitute a product bifurcation that lets AIXTRON address different substrate sizes, chemistries, and wafer-count economics across its tool catalogue.

## Process IP Across Material Systems

Each compound-semiconductor material system presents its own set of thermodynamic and chemical obstacles, and AIXTRON's process IP is stratified accordingly.

For **GaN-on-Si** power devices, the central challenge is managing the 17% thermal expansion mismatch between gallium nitride and silicon. Growing a crack-free, low-defect GaN stack on a 200mm silicon wafer requires a precisely engineered series of interlayers — aluminium nitride nucleation layers, aluminium gallium nitride step-graded buffers — whose composition and thickness profiles are the subject of proprietary process recipes embedded in the G5+ and G10-GaN tools. AIXTRON sells these recipes as part of the process package, not merely the hardware, which is a meaningful differentiator: a customer operating an AIXTRON G10-GaN receives validated process windows developed over years of internal and customer co-development, reducing the time to qualified production yield.

For **SiC homoepitaxy**, the physics are different in kind. Silicon carbide grows at temperatures above 1,500°C — roughly twice the growth temperature for GaN — and the chemistry involves chlorinated precursors that are corrosive to conventional reactor components. The G10-SiC platform, commercialised by 2023, required AIXTRON to develop susceptor materials, liner designs, and gas injection systems tolerant of those conditions. The IP around high-temperature SiC epitaxy thus extends into materials science — specifically the development of graphite and silicon carbide–coated components that maintain dimensional stability and do not introduce metallic contamination into the epi layer.

For **GaAs and InP** optoelectronic devices — laser diodes for datacom transceivers, automotive LiDAR chips, VCSELs for 3D sensing — AIXTRON's process IP centres on phosphorus handling (white phosphorus is pyrophoric and requires careful abatement), ultra-thin quantum well accuracy, and the multi-layer arsenide/phosphide structures that define device bandgap engineering. The ~~CCS platform has been the primary vehicle for these applications~~ ==current high-volume G10-AsP platform is Planetary Reactor based==, and the process knowledge embedded in tool configurations represents years of co-development with customers such as II-VI/Coherent and Lumentum.

## The Aachen Research Ecosystem

AIXTRON's headquarters in Herzogenrath, a small municipality on the German side of the Belgian border near Aachen, is not a historical accident. The proximity to RWTH Aachen — one of Europe's highest-ranked technical universities for electrical engineering and materials science — provides a sustained pipeline of doctoral researchers, joint projects, and informal intellectual exchange that the company has cultivated since its founding.

The company maintained research collaborations with Fraunhofer institutes, notably Fraunhofer IAF in Freiburg (III-V semiconductors and high-frequency devices) and Fraunhofer IISB in Erlangen (wide-bandgap power devices), using those partnerships to validate process capabilities against device-level electrical performance rather than purely film-quality metrics. This systems-level feedback loop — from reactor recipe to finished transistor — informed tool refinements that would not have emerged from internal epitaxy characterisation alone.

R&D expenditure as a share of revenue has historically run at approximately 10–12%, a ratio that management described as consistent with the company's strategy of sustaining IP leadership rather than competing on price. The engineering workforce is concentrated in Herzogenrath, with additional process and applications engineering in ~~Cambridge, United Kingdom — the legacy of AIXTRON's 2002 acquisition of Thomas Swan Scientific Equipment~~ ==Swavesey, Cambridge, United Kingdom — the legacy of AIXTRON's 1999 acquisition of Thomas Swan Scientific Equipment== — and in Santa Clara, California, serving North American and Korean customer bases.

## Patent Portfolio and Competitive Moat

AIXTRON's patent estate spans reactor geometry, gas distribution hardware, susceptor and satellite designs, thermal management systems, in-situ measurement methods (including reflectance-based growth-rate monitoring and emissivity-corrected pyrometry), and process sequences for specific material systems. The company has not disclosed aggregate patent counts in granular detail in its standard IR filings, but the portfolio accumulated across its four decades of operation represents a substantial barrier to imitation — not because any single patent is impenetrable, but because the interdependency of hardware, process chemistry, and software control creates a system whose replication requires simultaneous mastery of multiple disciplines.

Veeco Instruments, AIXTRON's principal competitor in MOCVD for power and photonics applications, pursues broadly similar deposition physics through different mechanical implementations — most notably its TurboDisc platform, which uses a different rotation geometry. The existence of two viable MOCVD architectures has prevented either company from achieving absolute monopoly, but AIXTRON's Planetary Reactor remains the dominant tool in GaN power production lines at the customers that have publicly disclosed their equipment choices.

The institutional memory encoded in AIXTRON's engineering organisation — the accumulated heuristics of growing compound semiconductors in production for four decades — may ultimately be more durable than any individual patent filing. That memory, rooted in the Aachen academic tradition and refined through thousands of customer process interactions, is the company's deepest competitive asset.

chapters.title: Capital-cycle cyclicality, China export controls, micro-LED uncertainty, FX, competitive, governance
chapters.body:
## The Capital Cycle's Long Shadow

AIXTRON's revenue history is, at its core, a ledger of compound-semiconductor investment waves. The first and most instructive was the LED MOCVD super-cycle of 2010–2012, when Chinese LED manufacturers absorbed hundreds of reactors in the space of roughly eighteen months and then stopped ordering almost as abruptly as they had started. Order intake collapsed, revenue fell sharply in subsequent years, and the company spent the better part of a decade reorienting its portfolio toward GaN power, SiC power, and photonics to escape the trough.

The GaN and SiC power inflection that drove AIXTRON to ~~a record €629.7 million in fiscal 2023 revenue~~==€629.9 million in fiscal 2023 revenue, below the LED-era fiscal 2010 peak== bore the same structural signature. Customers—Infineon, STMicroelectronics, Wolfspeed, Innoscience, and a cluster of Chinese power-device fabs—ordered reactors in clusters as they committed to new compound-semiconductor fabrication capacity. By 2024, enough of that initial capital programme had been absorbed that portions of the customer base entered a digestion phase, pausing new orders while running installed AIXTRON tools toward fuller utilisation. The company's own guidance and quarterly order-intake disclosures to Frankfurt Xetra reflected the consequent moderation, with fiscal 2024 revenue ~~tracking below the 2023 peak~~==roughly flat to slightly above fiscal 2023== even as the secular GaN adoption story remained intact. [AIXTRON IR disclosures](https://investors.aixtron.com)

The structural risk is the asymmetry of the order signal. A customer commissioning a new SiC fab may spend twelve months ordering and receiving tools, then run those tools for three to five years before ordering incremental capacity. AIXTRON's backlog and order intake—disclosed quarterly—are therefore coincident indicators of customer capital commitment rather than leading indicators of end-market demand. Even sustained GaN adoption growth can coexist with multi-quarter equipment order softness, and the market's valuation of AIXTRON tends to punish that softness harshly at the first sign of deceleration.

## China: The Licence Overhang

China has been among AIXTRON's most consequential customer geographies across multiple product cycles, from the LED MOCVD era through the more recent GaN and SiC power device buildout. In recent fiscal years, Chinese-sourced revenue represented a meaningful double-digit share of total group revenue—a concentration that became increasingly fraught as Western governments moved to constrain China's advanced semiconductor manufacturing capability.

From 2023 onward, German authorities, operating under the EU dual-use export control framework, required individual export licences for certain AIXTRON MOCVD tool shipments to China. The scope of the licensing requirement, the category of Chinese customers deemed eligible to receive equipment, and the timeline for licence approvals introduced an overhang on near-term China order conversion that AIXTRON could not resolve through commercial negotiation alone. The company's quarterly order disclosures were, in effect, a running scorecard of the licensing environment as well as underlying customer demand.

The deeper structural risk was not administrative but competitive. AMEC (Advanced Micro-Fabrication Equipment Inc.) and Naura Technology Group, both listed Chinese equipment makers with access to state-adjacent capital, have been investing systematically to develop domestic MOCVD capability for power electronics and photonics applications. Their near-term process performance lagged AIXTRON's G10 platform metrics on wafer uniformity and throughput—specifications that demanding GaN and SiC power device customers benchmark rigorously—but the gap was narrowing. A China that sources MOCVD equipment domestically represents not a temporary headwind but a permanent reduction in the addressable market for AIXTRON's China revenue. [AIXTRON Frankfurt Xetra AIXA.DE filings](https://investors.aixtron.com)

## The Micro-LED Thesis Deferred

Of the six principal risks, the micro-LED display thesis uncertainty carried the most visible optionality swing in AIXTRON's forward narrative. AIXTRON had invested substantially in positioning its MOCVD platforms as enabling infrastructure for micro-LED display epitaxy—a process requiring compound-semiconductor deposition at uniformity and yield specifications that exceeded those of conventional LED manufacturing by orders of magnitude.

The bull thesis rested, in large part, on Apple as the anchor demand signal. Apple Watch was, per supply-chain analysis and press reporting circulating from roughly 2020 onward, the candidate device for the first mass-market transition from OLED to micro-LED displays—a transition that would require substantial new MOCVD reactor capacity at display substrate makers. That scenario met a sharp reversal in early 2024 when multiple credible press reports indicated Apple had cancelled or indefinitely delayed the Apple Watch micro-LED programme, citing cost and yield challenges that remained unresolved at commercial scale.

The immediate commercial consequence for AIXTRON was the removal of a near-term order catalyst. Customers who had been evaluating MOCVD capacity for micro-LED production pulled back; the pipeline of display-related orders thinned. The medium-term risk is more insidious: each year of deferral is a year in which advanced OLED and mini-LED alternatives capture consumer device design wins and deepen incumbent supply chains. If mass micro-LED adoption has moved from a 2025–2027 window to a 2030-and-beyond scenario, the portion of AIXTRON's compound-annual-growth-rate assumption attributable to display applications requires material revision.

## Currency: Structural Translation Drag

AIXTRON's financial architecture creates a persistent asymmetry between where it earns and where it spends. The company reports in euros; its cost base—engineering staff, manufacturing, and administration in Herzogenrath and the Aachen corridor—is predominantly euro-denominated. Its revenue, by contrast, flows from customers in the United States, China, Korea, Japan, Taiwan, and across Southeast Asia, where billing currencies include US dollars, renminbi, won, and yen.

Euro appreciation against any of these currencies compresses reported revenue and margin without any underlying change in volume or pricing. A sustained ten-percentage-point euro strengthening against the US dollar—not an unusual move over a multi-year cycle—mechanically reduces reported EUR revenue from dollar-billings by a corresponding margin. Because the cost base does not deflate symmetrically, the margin effect is amplified rather than offset. AIXTRON can hedge near-term transaction exposures but cannot structurally eliminate translation drag without relocating cost structure—an option that conflicts with its German engineering and manufacturing identity. FX is, accordingly, a chronic source of reported-earnings volatility that obscures underlying operational performance. [AIXTRON Annual Report](https://investors.aixtron.com)

## Competitive Intensity: East and West

AIXTRON's MOCVD franchise is the dominant European position in its niche, but competition from two directions was intensifying through the frozen window.

| Competitor | Geography | Relevant platform | Competitive vector |
|---|---|---|---|
| Veeco Instruments | USA | Propel (GaN power MOCVD) | US customer relationships; ITAR/supply-chain-risk framing for domestic defence/power buyers |
| AMEC | China | Domestic GaN / compound-semi tools | China market localisation; state-supported pricing |
| Naura Technology | China | Compound-semi epi equipment | Vertically integrated Chinese fab customer relationships |

Veeco represents the most direct process-performance competition in the near term. Its Propel platform targets the same GaN-on-Si and GaN-on-SiC power device applications as AIXTRON's G10-GaN tool, and its US domicile is a commercial advantage in procurement decisions influenced by supply-chain sovereignty considerations—including US defence and data-centre customers who may favour domestic equipment vendors. Veeco's scale, however, remained smaller than AIXTRON's through the frozen window, limiting its ability to match AIXTRON's installed-base density and customer intimacy in the field.

The AMEC and Naura vector is a longer-horizon risk with potentially larger magnitude. Both companies benefited from the Chinese government's explicit equipment self-sufficiency programme, accessing capital at terms that Western capital markets would not replicate. Their strategy—first to capture domestic Chinese customers with good-enough tools at lower cost, then to expand into third-country markets—tracked the historical trajectory of other Chinese equipment categories. AIXTRON's competitive moat in this scenario depends on maintaining a durable process-performance lead: if its tool platforms run GaN or SiC device epitaxy at meaningfully higher yields or throughput than Chinese alternatives, domestic substitution is slow. If that gap narrows faster than expected, the margin at which AIXTRON can price globally compresses.

## Governance and the ~~SDAX~~==MDAX/TecDAX== Constraint

AIXTRON operates within Germany's two-tier corporate governance model: an Executive Board (Vorstand) responsible for strategy and management, supervised by a Supervisory Board (Aufsichtsrat) responsible for oversight and remuneration. Following Bernd Schulte's ~~retirement at the end of 2023 after a multi-decade tenure as co-CEO, Felix Grawert assumed sole leadership of the Executive Board~~==departure from the Executive Board in 2021, Felix Grawert, who joined the Executive Board in August 2017, has served as Chairman of the Executive Board, CEO & President since March 2021==—a consolidation of executive authority appropriate for a company of AIXTRON's size but one that concentrates strategic decision-making in a single leader whose views on product roadmap and capital allocation are largely determinative.

AIXTRON's ~~SDAX membership~~==MDAX and TecDAX membership== on Frankfurt Xetra imposes a liquidity and institutional-ownership constraint that its larger German technology peers in the DAX ~~or MDAX~~ do not share. Many global asset managers operate benchmark mandates that ~~do not extend below DAX or MDAX inclusion thresholds, structurally narrowing~~==differentiate between DAX large-cap exposure and mid-cap or technology-index exposure, shaping== the buyer pool and amplifying valuation volatility on material news. Order-intake disclosures, export-licence developments, or macro risk-off episodes affecting ~~small-cap~~==mid-cap== technology names can move AIXTRON's share price by percentages that would be moderated in a larger-cap structure with deeper institutional float. This is not a governance failure but a structural feature of the company's market position—a persistent discount embedded in the cost of equity that only a sustained earnings track record or ~~index-level reclassification upward~~==larger-cap index profile== would resolve. [AIXTRON AIXA.DE, Frankfurt Xetra](https://investors.aixtron.com)

Taken together, the six risk dimensions form an interlocking constraint on AIXTRON's forward earnings visibility: cyclicality determines revenue amplitude, China determines near-term volume, micro-LED determines the upside option, FX determines reported margin, competition determines long-term pricing power, and governance determines the rate at which the market discounts the residual uncertainty. None of these risks is novel to the business; what distinguishes the 2024–2026 period is their simultaneous activation across the same compressed window.

chapters.title: The next 12 months — catalysts, estimates, and what to watch
chapters.body:
## The catalyst clock, May 2026 to May 2027

With the Q1 2026 earnings cycle behind it, AIXTRON enters ~~the first full operating year of Felix Grawert's sole-CEO tenure~~ ==another operating year under Felix Grawert, CEO & President since March 2021== at an inflection that is genuine but not yet confirmed by the order book. The ~~GaN power cycle that drove the company's revenue above €600m in fiscal 2024 has moved through the first phase of its digestion: Chinese device makers absorbed capacity aggressively in 2022 and 2023, paused orders through much of 2024 and into early 2025, and by late 2025 had begun signalling renewed tool procurement interest~~ ==near-term demand signal at the snapshot was optoelectronics-led: FY2025 revenue contracted 12% to €556.6m, order intake fell 9% to €544.3m, and AIXTRON's April 2026 update framed GaN as stable to moderate and SiC as weak because of overcapacity==. The ~~SiC power platform has found its first production customers but faces a more established competitive field than GaN did~~ ==SiC power platform remains strategic, but the next 12 months must show that weak customer capex can turn into orders rather than only qualification activity==. The micro-LED thesis, stripped of the Apple Watch programme that anchored its near-term revenue case, has migrated from a 2024–2025 catalyst to a longer-dated option. What follows is a quarter-by-quarter map of the events and data releases that will confirm — or break — the ~~recovery story~~ ==optoelectronics-led guidance framework and any FY2027 growth story== between now and May 2027.

## Earnings calendar and milestone map

AIXTRON reports on a calendar fiscal year. Based on the company's established reporting cadence, the following schedule applies to the frozen-snapshot window:

| Date (approximate) | Event | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Late July 2026 | H1 2026 / Q2 2026 results | First full look at whether Q2 order intake sustains the Q1 recovery signal |

The single most important date in this sequence is the FY2026 full-year result and 2027 guidance release, expected around ~~late February or early~~ ==March== 2027. AIXTRON's revenue lags its order book by roughly two to three quarters — so a genuine FY2027 growth story must be visible in H2 2026 order intake before the guidance is published.

## Consensus estimates

The following ~~estimates represent the FactSet / Bloomberg analyst consensus as of the frozen snapshot, with management's own guidance range as the anchor~~ ==figures separate AIXTRON's actual reported FY2025/Q1 2026 data and issued 2026 guidance from analyst-derived out-period estimates==. AIXTRON guides revenue plus EBIT margin (not EPS directly); EPS is an analyst-derived figure from those two inputs.

| Period | Revenue (€m) | Y/Y growth | EBIT margin | EBIT (€m) | EPS (€) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FY2025A | ~~\~€555–580m~~ ==€556.6m== | ~~\~−8 to −12%~~ ==−12%== | ~~\~20–22%~~ ==18%== | ~~\~€115–125m~~ ==€100.3m== | ~~\~€0.76–0.83~~ ==—== |

| Q3 2026E | ~€158–172m | +high-teens | ~23% | ~€36–40m | ~€0.24 |
| Q4 2026E | ~€168–185m | +~20% | ~24% | ~€40–44m | ~€0.27 |
| FY2026E | ~~\~€610–660m~~ ==around €560m plus/minus €30m guidance== | ~~+\~8–15%~~ ==roughly −5% to +6%== | ~~\~22–24%~~ ==around 17–20%== | ~~\~€134–158m~~ ==~€90–118m== | ~~\~€0.88–1.04~~ ==—== |
